verses.1: Al-Mizan traces ṭāriq from a sharp audible blow, whence miṭraqah, a hammer, and ṭarīq, a path struck by travellers' feet. It came to denote travel, especially nocturnal arrival when one knocks at a closed door, and then any night occurrence. Here al-ṭāriq is a star rising at night, and the verse is an oath by the sky and that star.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says the question intensifies and emphasizes what is sworn by: al-ṭāriq, the nightly visitor.
verses.3: Al-Mizan explains al-thāqib as the brilliant star. Thaqb conveys piercing and tearing, and thus brilliance that pierces darkness, as well as height and elevation, like a bird tearing through the air as it soars. The verse answers the implied question about al-ṭāriq in (86:1-2) by identifying it as this star.
verses.4: Al-Mizan takes lammā as illā: every soul has a ḥāfiẓ, a guardian angel recording its good and evil acts for Resurrection accounting, as in (82:10-12). It also considers a generic preservation of each soul's essence and deeds: at death neither perishes, and God returns the same soul at resurrection for recompense, a reading compatible with angels as recorders and with (32:11), (39:42), and (45:29). Against the objection that a recreated body could only be a copy, the commentary replies that the soul, not the body, is the person's reality. Joining the preserved soul to a new body therefore restores the identical person, even if that body resembles the former one.
verses.5: Al-Mizan reads the initial faʾ as the conclusion of the preceding preservation of souls and deeds: people must acknowledge their return to God and recompense rather than deem it unlikely. Reflection on their origin from a fluid issuing between loins and ribs shows that the One who began human creation from a drop can restore life after death. The passive ‘he was created’ leaves the Creator unnamed because His agency is evident; the same applies in (86:6).
verses.6: Al-Mizan defines dāfiq as rapidly pouring or flowing and identifies the effusing fluid as semen. Ṣulb means loins or back, while tarāʾib is the plural of tarībah, breastbones or ribs; despite extensive disagreement, the phrase apparently denotes the bodily region bounded by the loins and chest bones. An editorial note adds that tirb may denote paired bones and can be read as the thighbones, making the phrase a courteous allusion to the male organ; the author's note refers readers to al-Marāghī for a medically subtle account.

verses.8: Al-Mizan defines rajʿ as iʿādah, returning or restoring. Although the preceding verses do not name God, the pronoun is sufficient because His agency is evident, just as the prior passive forms make it evident; the One who created from that fluid can restore a person after death, since restoration resembles first creation. The return occurs when al-sarāʾir—hidden intentions—are tublā, examined and disclosed: concealed beliefs and the consequences of good and evil deeds are revealed, distinguished, and recompensed, as in (2:284). Then no one has either personal power or a helper to avert the consequences of those beliefs and deeds or God's punishment.

verses.11: Al-Mizan treats the paired oaths as confirmation of resurrection and return to God. Heaven's rajʿ is the recurring cycle of stars rising and setting, though rainfall cycles are also suggested; the earth's splitting is its cleaving as plants grow. Both images make clear the return of the dead and their emergence from graves.

verses.13: Al-Mizan identifies ‘it’ as the Qur'an, not the previously mentioned resurrection. Faṣl is a distinction that separates, while hazl is the opposite of jidd, seriousness. The oaths therefore affirm that the Qur'an decisively separates truth from falsehood and is no jest: what it affirms, including resurrection and return, is certainly true, and what it rejects is false. The commentary records the alternative referent but judges its own reading more plausible; an author's note explains the verbal-noun form faṣl as emphatic for the active sense ‘distinguishing.’

verses.15: Al-Mizan says the faithless plot through disbelief and denial of the hereafter to extinguish God's light and nullify the Prophet's call. Their very plotting becomes God's plot against them: He grants respite that lets them deepen their ruin, permits them to sink fully into misguidance, seals their hearts, and veils their hearing and sight, culminating in eternal punishment.

verses.17: Al-Mizan calls tamhīl and imhāl synonymous forms of granting respite, but distinguishes the former as gradual and the latter as a sudden single act; ruwayda means a little while. The Prophet is told to be patient and not hurry the faithless, for their plot is God's counterplot and God has full command of His affairs (12:21); what is promised is practically near. An author's note sees ‘a little’ with the sudden verb as indicating the punishment's imminence, and an editor identifies the final maxim as a widely reported Prophetic narration and proverb.
